entries.content:
Many AI agent tutorials start with a language model, give it a few tools, and run a loop until it produces an answer. That's enough to demonstrate tool calling, but it leaves the interesting engineering questions unanswered.

What happens when a tool fails? Who validates the arguments? What prevents an agent from running indefinitely, executing unsafe commands, or exhausting its context window? And how do you test any of this without relying on unpredictable model responses?

These are responsibilities of the agent harness: the software that sits between a language model and the environment it operates in.

In this tutorial, we'll build a small, provider-independent harness in TypeScript, using a coding agent as our example. We'll start with a basic execution loop and progressively add tool validation, workspace isolation, execution budgets, context management, observability, and deterministic failure testing.

What We'll Cover

Prerequisites

Familiarity with TypeScript and basic knowledge of AI agents will be helpful. We'll use Node.js 24, TypeScript, and its built-in test runner, with minimal dependencies.

The complete implementation is available in the companion repository: agent-harness-from-scratch. Each section corresponds to a Git tag, so you can follow the project as it develops instead of starting with the final code.

1. Build the Basic Agent Loop

To follow along, check out the initial milestone:

git clone https://github.com/gkoos/agent-harness-from-scratch.git
cd agent-harness-from-scratch
git switch --detach 01-model-loop
npm ci
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run demo

The detached checkout puts you at the exact snapshot discussed here without moving a branch. When you reach the next section, switch to its tag. You'll need Node.js 24 and npm installed.

The most important architectural decision is that the model proposes actions while the harness executes them. When a model requests a tool call, it hasn't actually executed anything. It has generated a structured request containing a tool name and arguments. The harness must interpret that request, invoke the corresponding implementation, and return the result to the model.

The interaction looks like this:

We'll start by defining the contracts in 

src/core/types.ts
.

export type ToolCall = { id: string; name: string; arguments: unknown };

export type Message =
  | { role: 'user'; content: string }
  | { role: 'assistant'; content: string; toolCalls?: ToolCall[] }
  | { role: 'tool'; callId: string; content: string; isError: boolean };

export interface ToolDefinition {
  name: string;
  description: string;
  parameters: Record; // JSON Schema for the model
}

export interface Tool extends ToolDefinition {
  execute(argumentsValue: unknown, signal: AbortSignal): Promise;
}

export interface Model {
  generate(input: {
    messages: readonly Message[];
    tools: readonly ToolDefinition[];
    signal: AbortSignal;
  }): Promise<{ content: string; toolCalls?: ToolCall[] }>;
}

export type AgentResult = {
  status: 'completed' | 'step_limit' | 'aborted';
  answer?: string;
  messages: Message[];
  steps: number;
};

The 

Model
interface deliberately contains nothing specific to OpenAI, Anthropic, or any other provider. A provider adapter can translate between its API and these types without changing the harness.

Notice that tool arguments are 

unknown
, not 
any
. Model-generated data is untrusted input. We'll validate it before execution in the next section.

The agent loop in 

src/core/agent.ts
follows a simple sequence:

  • Send the conversation and available tool definitions to the model.

  • Append the model's response to the conversation.

  • If it requested tools, execute them and append their results.

  • Repeat until the model returns a final answer or the harness reaches its step limit.

Here is the complete initial loop in 

src/core/agent.ts
. The model receives tool definitions, while the harness retains the executable implementations:
import type { AgentResult, Message, Model, Tool } from './types.ts';

export async function runAgent(options: {
  model: Model;
  tools: readonly Tool[];
  prompt: string;
  maxSteps?: number;
  signal?: AbortSignal;
}): Promise {
  const { model, tools, prompt, maxSteps = 10 } = options;
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(maxSteps) || maxSteps < 1) {
    throw new RangeError('maxSteps must be a positive safe integer');
  }
  const signal = options.signal ?? new AbortController().signal;
  const messages: Message[] = [{ role: 'user', content: prompt }];
  const registry = new Map(tools.map(tool => [tool.name, tool]));
  if (registry.size !== tools.length) throw new Error('Duplicate tool names');
  const definitions = tools.map(({ name, description, parameters }) => ({ name, description, parameters }));

  for (let step = 0; step < maxSteps; step++) {
    if (signal.aborted) return { status: 'aborted', messages, steps: step };
    let response;
    try {
      response = await model.generate({ messages: [...messages], tools: definitions, signal });
    } catch (error) {
      if (signal.aborted) return { status: 'aborted', messages, steps: step };
      throw error;
    }
    if (signal.aborted) return { status: 'aborted', messages, steps: step };
    const calls = response.toolCalls ?? [];
    messages.push({ role: 'assistant', content: response.content, ...(calls.length ? { toolCalls: calls } : {}) });
    if (!calls.length) return { status: 'completed', answer: response.content, messages, steps: step + 1 };

    for (const call of calls) {
      if (signal.aborted) return { status: 'aborted', messages, steps: step + 1 };
      const tool = registry.get(call.name);
      if (!tool) {
        messages.push({ role: 'tool', callId: call.id, content: `Unknown tool: ${call.name}`, isError: true });
        continue;
      }
      try {
        const result = await tool.execute(call.arguments, signal);
        if (signal.aborted) return { status: 'aborted', messages, steps: step + 1 };
        messages.push({ role: 'tool', callId: call.id, content: JSON.stringify(result) ?? 'null', isError: false });
      } catch (error) {
        if (signal.aborted) return { status: 'aborted', messages, steps: step + 1 };
        messages.push({
          role: 'tool', callId: call.id,
          content: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error),
          isError: true
        });
      }
    }
  }
  return { status: 'step_limit', messages, steps: maxSteps };
}

A response without tool calls ends the run. Otherwise, the harness looks up each requested tool and executes it.

Tool failures don't automatically terminate the agent. Instead, the harness records an error message associated with the original call ID. This allows the model to react to a missing file or failed operation on its next turn.

We also impose a maximum number of model turns. A model can keep requesting work, but it doesn't get to decide how much execution time or how many iterations it's entitled to.

Test Without a Real Model

Rather than making nondeterministic API calls in tests (and burning tokens or GPU power), we introduce a scripted fake model in 

src/models/fake.ts
. It returns predefined responses: first a tool request, then a final answer.

The fake model advances through an array of responses. Exhausting the script is an error, so an unexpected extra model turn won't silently pass:

// src/models/fake.ts
import type { Model } from '../core/types.ts';

export function scriptedModel(
  responses: Array>>
): Model {
  let index = 0;
  return {
    async generate() {
      const response = responses[index++];
      if (!response) throw new Error('Scripted model exhausted');
      return response;
    }
  };
}

Here's a minimal test for 

tests/agent.test.ts
. Run it with 
npm test
:
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { runAgent } from '../src/core/agent.ts';
import { scriptedModel } from '../src/models/fake.ts';

test('executes a tool and returns the final answer', async () => {
  const result = await runAgent({
    prompt: 'Say hello',
    tools: [{
      name: 'hello', description: 'Return a greeting',
      parameters: { type: 'object' },
      async execute() { return 'Hello'; }
    }],
    model: scriptedModel([
      { content: '', toolCalls: [{ id: '1', name: 'hello', arguments: {} }] },
      { content: 'Done' }
    ])
  });
  assert.equal(result.status, 'completed');
  assert.equal(result.answer, 'Done');
  assert.deepEqual(result.messages[2], {
    role: 'tool', callId: '1', content: '"Hello"', isError: false
  });
});

The companion demo uses the same pattern. Additional tests cover unknown tools, step limits, and cancellation without API keys, network access, or token costs.

At this point, we have a working agent loop, but it still trusts model-generated tool arguments and has no meaningful restrictions on what registered tools can do.

2. Validate Tool Calls Before Executing Them

Our first loop lets the model request a tool by name, then passes its arguments directly to the implementation. That works for a demo, but the tool description is only a request to the model, it isn't a guarantee that the model will return valid arguments.

For this section, check out the second milestone of the companion repository:

git switch --detach 02-tool-dispatch

This tag adds 

src/core/registry.ts
, which handles tool registration and runtime argument validation. It also changes the failure behavior in 
src/core/agent.ts
.

A Registry with Explicit Contracts

The 

ToolRegistry
replaces the initial loop's plain 
Map
. It rejects invalid or duplicate tool names and exposes only the definitions the model needs:
import type { Tool, ToolDefinition } from './types.ts';

export class ToolRegistry {
  private readonly tools = new Map();
  constructor(tools: readonly Tool[]) {
    for (const tool of tools) {
      if (!/^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_-]*$/.test(tool.name)) throw new Error(`Invalid tool name: ${tool.name}`);
      if (this.tools.has(tool.name)) throw new Error(`Duplicate tool name: ${tool.name}`);
      this.tools.set(tool.name, tool);
    }
  }
  definitions(): ToolDefinition[] {
    return [...this.tools.values()].map(({ name, description, parameters }) => ({ name, description, parameters }));
  }
  get(name: string): Tool | undefined { return this.tools.get(name); }
}

Create it with 

const registry = new ToolRegistry(tools)
and obtain the model-facing definitions with 
registry.definitions()
. When a response requests a tool, validate the supplied arguments before calling 
execute
:
const tool = registry.get(call.name);
if (!tool) {
  messages.push({
    role: 'tool', callId: call.id,
    content: `Unknown tool: ${call.name}`, isError: true
  });
  continue;
}

const validationErrors = validate(call.arguments, tool.parameters);
if (validationErrors.length) {
  messages.push({
    role: 'tool', callId: call.id,
    content: `Invalid arguments: ${validationErrors.join('; ')}`,
    isError: true
  });
  continue;
}

This is a critical boundary. 

arguments: unknown
remains untrusted until the harness checks it. If validation fails, the tool never runs. The model instead receives an error result associated with its original call ID.

The tutorial's 

validate
function supports a deliberately small JSON Schema subset: primitive and container 
type
checks, object 
properties
, 
required
fields, 
additionalProperties: false
, array 
items
, and 
enum
. It reports paths such as 
$.flags[0]
to help identify malformed input. It's not a complete JSON Schema implementation, and it doesn't validate tool schemas at registration time.

Here's the validator used above. It first checks the declared type, then recursively checks object properties and array items:

export function validate(value: unknown, schema: Record, path = '$'): string[] {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  const type = schema.type;
  if (typeof type !== 'string') return [`${path}: schema must declare a type`];
  const matches = type === 'object' ? value !== null && typeof value === 'object' && !Array.isArray(value)
    : type === 'array' ? Array.isArray(value)
    : type === 'integer' ? typeof value === 'number' && Number.isInteger(value)
    : type === 'number' ? typeof value === 'number' && Number.isFinite(value)
    : type === 'null' ? value === null
    : type === 'string' || type === 'boolean' ? typeof value === type : false;
  if (!matches) return [`${path}: expected ${type}`];
  if (Array.isArray(schema.enum) && !schema.enum.some(item => Object.is(item, value))) {
    errors.push(`${path}: not an allowed value`);
  }
  if (type === 'object') {
    const obj = value as Record;
    const properties = (schema.properties ?? {}) as Record>;
    for (const key of (schema.required ?? []) as string[]) {
      if (!Object.hasOwn(obj, key)) errors.push(`${path}.${key}: required`);
    }
    for (const [key, item] of Object.entries(obj)) {
      if (Object.hasOwn(properties, key)) errors.push(...validate(item, properties[key]!, `${path}.${key}`));
      else if (schema.additionalProperties === false) errors.push(`${path}.${key}: unexpected property`);
    }
  }
  if (type === 'array' && schema.items && typeof schema.items === 'object') {
    (value as unknown[]).forEach((item, index) => {
      errors.push(...validate(
        item, schema.items as Record, `${path}[${index}]`
      ));
    });
  }
  return errors;
}

Not Every Error Means the Same Thing

Milestone 2 also makes an important distinction between tool failure and model failure.

An unknown tool, invalid arguments, or an exception thrown by a tool becomes a 

role: 'tool'
message with 
isError: true
. The model can inspect that result and try something else on its next turn. By contrast, if 
model.generate()
itself throws, the harness terminates with 
status: 'model_error'
and records the error message.

This isn't just bookkeeping. A missing file might be recoverable, but an unavailable model provider means there's no model response to guide recovery. The harness shouldn't pretend these are the same situation.

In the loop's existing 

model.generate()
catch block, replace the rethrow with a structured outcome, and add 
'model_error'
and an optional 
error?: string
field to 
AgentResult
:
if (signal.aborted) return { status: 'aborted', messages, steps: step };
return {
  status: 'model_error', messages, steps: step,
  error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)
};

The tool execution catch block still records an error message and continues the loop.

The deterministic tests make that distinction concrete. In 

tests/agent.test.ts
, an invalid 

echo
argument is rejected without invoking the tool, while a thrown tool exception still allows the scripted model to return a final answer. 
tests/registry.test.ts
 checks nested argument validation and unexpected properties.

3. Give the Agent Tools Without Giving It the Machine

So far, our agent can request tools and the harness validates their arguments. But validation only establishes that a request has the right shape. A valid request to read 

../../secrets.txt
is still a request we should refuse.

Check out Milestone 3 in the companion repository:

git switch --detach 03-workspace-tools

This milestone adds workspace file tools and a restricted command tool. Neither depends on a particular model provider.

Confine File Operations to a Workspace

A coding agent needs to read and edit files, but it shouldn't automatically receive access to the entire filesystem. The 

Workspace
class resolves a canonical root when it's created:
const workspace = await Workspace.open('/path/to/project');
const tools = workspaceTools(workspace);

The resulting 

read_file
and 
write_file
tools accept paths relative to that root. Before opening a file, 
Workspace
rejects absolute paths, paths escaping the root, and symbolic links in existing path components. Writes require the parent directory to exist. The tool doesn't create arbitrary directory trees.

These two methods inside 

Workspace
enforce the path checks. The file imports 
isAbsolute
, 
relative
, and 
resolve
from 
node:path
, and 
lstat
and 
realpath
from 
node:fs/promises
. 
Workspace.open()
stores 
await realpath(root)
as 
this.root
:
private lexical(path: string): string {
    if (!path || isAbsolute(path)) throw new Error('Expected a relative workspace path');
    const full = resolve(this.root, path);
    const rel = relative(this.root, full);
    if (!rel || rel === '..' || rel.startsWith(`..${process.platform === 'win32' ? '\\' : '/'}`) || isAbsolute(rel)) {
      throw new Error('Path is outside the workspace or refers to its root');
    }
    return full;
  }

  /** Reject symlinks in every existing component, not just the final file. */
  private async check(path: string, allowMissingFinal: boolean): Promise {
    const full = this.lexical(path);
    const rel = relative(this.root, full);
    const parts = rel.split(/[\\/]/);
    let current = this.root;
    for (let i = 0; i < parts.length; i++) {
      current = resolve(current, parts[i]!);
      try {
        const stat = await lstat(current);
        if (stat.isSymbolicLink()) throw new Error('Symbolic links are not permitted');
        if (i < parts.length - 1 && !stat.isDirectory()) throw new Error('Parent is not a directory');
      } catch (error) {
        if (allowMissingFinal && i === parts.length - 1 && (error as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === 'ENOENT') break;
        throw error;
      }
    }
    return full;
  }


read
calls 
this.check(path, false)
before opening an existing file. 
write
calls 
this.check(path, true)
, which allows only the final file to be missing. A missing parent directory or any symlink still fails the check.

The boundary is enforced by the tool implementation, not by asking the model to behave. A model can request 

../secret.txt
, but the workspace refuses to open it. The harness then reports the failure as a recoverable tool result, just as it did for invalid arguments in Milestone 2.

For an additional check, the implementation opens files with 

O_NOFOLLOW
where supported, to avoid following a symbolic link at the final path component. That doesn't eliminate every race: directory components can change between checking and opening them. This is a useful educational restriction, not an OS-level sandbox.

Let the Model Choose Commands, Not Invent Them

Running commands is even more sensitive. Rather than accept a shell string generated by the model, we register named command presets:

const tool = commandTool(projectRoot, {
  test: {
    executable: process.execPath,
    args: ['--test', 'tests/example.test.js']
  }
});

The model can request 

{ "command": "test" }
, but it can't supply a different executable, extra arguments, or shell syntax. The command tool's dispatch boundary looks like this (inside its 
execute(value, signal)
method):
signal.throwIfAborted();
const name = (value as { command: string }).command;
if (!Object.hasOwn(presets, name)) throw new Error('Command not permitted');
const preset = presets[name]!;
const timeout = preset.timeoutMs ?? 10_000;
if (!Number.isSafeInteger(timeout) || timeout < 1) {
  throw new Error('Invalid timeout');
}

// Inside the Promise that collects the command's result:
const child = spawn(preset.executable, [...preset.args], {
  cwd, shell: false, signal, windowsHide: true,
  stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe']
});
const timer = setTimeout(() => child.kill(), timeout);

Here 

spawn
comes from 
node:child_process
, 
cwd
is the configured project root, and 
presets
is the developer-supplied map above. The result handlers collect stdout and stderr, kill the child if either captured string exceeds 65,536 characters, and clear 
timer
on error or close. The implementation measures JavaScript string length, rather than an exact byte count.

This reduces the number of commands the model can select, but it doesn't make the selected commands harmless. A test script can itself read files, access the network, or launch child processes. Killing a timed-out child also doesn't reliably terminate its entire process tree. Running untrusted repositories still requires process isolation, such as a properly configured container or OS sandbox.

The Milestone 3 tests cover normal reads and writes, traversal attempts, symbolic links, recoverable access failures, and rejected command names.

4. Put Limits on Execution

Our agent can now call validated tools, including workspace-aware file operations and predefined commands. But a valid operation isn't necessarily one we should allow indefinitely. A model could request hundreds of tool calls, or a command could hang while the agent waits for its result.

In this milestone, we make execution limits a harness responsibility rather than something we ask the model to respect.

Follow along with the exact repository version:

git switch --detach 04-execution-limits

If you haven't cloned the project yet, start with 

git clone https://github.com/gkoos/agent-harness-from-scratch.git
and 
cd agent-harness-from-scratch
.

Count Turns and Tool Calls Separately

The original 

maxSteps
setting limits model responses, not the number of tool calls. One response can request several tools, so a turn limit alone doesn't bound the amount of work.

We extend 

runAgent
with two additional options:

const result = await runAgent({
  model,
  tools,
  prompt: 'Check the project',
  maxSteps: 10,
  maxToolCalls: 30,
  timeoutMs: 15_000
});

Every requested call consumes the tool-call budget, including unknown tools and calls with invalid arguments. This matters because even failed requests consume harness work. Initialize 

let toolCalls = 0
before the loop, then increment it immediately before looking up each admitted call's tool. That placement counts rejected arguments and unknown tools too.

The model may also return multiple tool calls at once. Instead of executing the first few and then discovering that the budget has run out, the harness checks whether the entire batch fits:

if (calls.length > maxToolCalls - toolCalls) {
  return { status: 'tool_limit', messages, steps, toolCalls };
}

This prevents budget-driven partial execution. It doesn't make the batch transactional: a tool can still fail, or execution can be cancelled partway through.

Propagate Cancellation and Deadlines

A caller can supply an 

AbortSignal
, while 
timeoutMs
creates an internal deadline. The harness combines these through an 
AbortController
and passes its signal to the model and tools.

The setup replaces the initial loop's directly selected signal:

const controller = new AbortController();
let timedOut = false;
const => controller.abort(options.signal?.reason);
if (options.signal?.aborted) onAbort();
else options.signal?.addEventListener('abort', onAbort, { once: true });
const timer = timeoutMs === undefined ? undefined : setTimeout(() => {
  timedOut = true;
  controller.abort(new Error('Agent deadline exceeded'));
}, timeoutMs);
const signal = controller.signal;

Pass this 

signal
to 
model.generate()
and 
tool.execute()
, as in the original loop. Wrap the loop in 
try
/
finally
so completion and early returns both release the timer and listener:
try {
  // The execution loop goes here, using controller.signal.
} finally {
  if (timer !== undefined) clearTimeout(timer);
  options.signal?.removeEventListener('abort', onAbort);
}

At execution boundaries, check 

signal.aborted
and return 
timedOut ? 'timeout' : 'aborted'
as the status. The result also reports 
steps
and 
toolCalls
, so callers can see how much work happened before termination.

This is cooperative cancellation, not forced termination. If an adapter ignores its signal, a pending operation may outlive the deadline. Likewise, killing a child process doesn't necessarily stop its descendants. A hard execution boundary requires process or container isolation.

Test the Limits Without Waiting for Real Failures

The 

budget tests
use the scripted model to request an over-budget batch and verify that zero tools execute. Other tests check that invalid requests consume budget, a pre-aborted signal prevents model invocation, and cooperative models and tools stop on deadlines.

The result types in 

types.ts
now distinguish 

completed
, 
step_limit
, 
tool_limit
, 
aborted
, 
timeout
, and 
model_error
. These outcomes are deliberately different: a run can stop correctly without completing the user's task.

5. Keep the Context Under Control

The harness now has limits on how long it can run, but its conversation keeps growing. Every model response and tool result becomes another message sent back to the model. A single file read could return thousands of lines. Several iterations can exhaust a model's context window long before the step budget is reached.

Milestone 5 introduces a distinction between the transcript we retain and the messages we send to the model. Check out the implementation:

git switch --detach 05-context

The relevant files are 

src/core/context.ts
, 
src/core/agent.ts
, and 
tests/context.test.ts
.

Bound Tool Output and Model-Facing History

The new 

context
option sets two separate limits:
const result = await runAgent({
  prompt: 'Inspect the project',
  model,
  tools,
  context: {
    maxContextChars: 32_000,
    maxToolResultChars: 8_000
  }
});


maxToolResultChars
bounds each tool result before it enters the transcript. Oversized results retain their beginning and end, with an omission marker in the middle. The discarded portion isn't available later, even in 
result.messages
.

The truncation helper reserves room for the marker, then divides the remaining space between the beginning and end:

export function boundToolResult(content: string, limit: number): string {
  if (content.length <= limit) return content;
  const marker = `\n...[${content.length - limit} or more characters omitted]...\n`;
  if (marker.length >= limit) return marker.slice(0, limit);
  const remaining = limit - marker.length;
  const front = Math.ceil(remaining / 2);
  const back = Math.floor(remaining / 2);
  return content.slice(0, front) + marker + (back ? content.slice(-back) : '');
}

Apply it when recording both successful results and error strings: 

content: boundToolResult(content, context.maxToolResultChars)
. This compact version explicitly handles a zero-length tail so 
slice(-0)
can't accidentally retain the whole result.

maxContextChars
limits the serialized message array passed to the model. The harness retains older messages in its returned transcript, but 
selectContext()
sends the initial user request plus as many recent turns as fit. There's no summarization: omitted history is simply unavailable to the model on that turn.

These are character limits, not token limits. They measure JavaScript string length after JSON serialization, excluding tool definitions and provider-specific overhead. A real provider adapter would need token-aware accounting and space reserved for the response.

Don't Split a Tool Call From its Result

Context trimming isn't as simple as removing the oldest messages. An assistant response may request several tools, each identified by a call ID. Sending only some of their results would create an invalid or misleading conversation.

The selector therefore treats the assistant message and all results from that batch as an indivisible group. It either includes the complete group or omits it. It also rejects orphaned results and incomplete batches rather than quietly constructing inconsistent context.

Here's 

selectContext()
from 
src/core/context.ts
, using the 
Message
type defined in Section 1. The first loop validates and groups the transcript. The second walks backward through whole groups until the budget is full:
import type { Message } from './types.ts';

const size = (messages: readonly Message[]) => JSON.stringify(messages).length;

export function selectContext(messages: readonly Message[], maxChars: number): Message[] {
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(maxChars) || maxChars < 1) {
    throw new RangeError('maxContextChars must be a positive safe integer');
  }
  if (!messages.length) return [];
  const groups: Message[][] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < messages.length;) {
    const message = messages[i]!;
    if (message.role === 'assistant' && message.toolCalls?.length) {
      const ids = new Set(message.toolCalls.map(call => call.id));
      if (ids.size !== message.toolCalls.length) throw new Error('Duplicate tool call IDs in assistant turn');
      const group: Message[] = [message];
      i++;
      while (i < messages.length && messages[i]!.role === 'tool') {
        const result = messages[i]!;
        if (result.role === 'tool' && !ids.delete(result.callId)) throw new Error('Orphan or duplicate tool result');
        group.push(result);
        i++;
      }
      if (ids.size) throw new Error('Incomplete tool result batch');
      groups.push(group);
    } else {
      if (message.role === 'tool') throw new Error('Orphan tool result');
      groups.push([message]);
      i++;
    }
  }
  const first = groups[0]!;
  if (first[0]?.role !== 'user') throw new Error('Conversation must start with a user message');
  const recent: Message[][] = [];
  for (let i = groups.length - 1; i >= 1; i--) {
    const group = groups[i]!;
    const next = [...first, ...[group, ...recent].flat()];
    if (size(next) > maxChars) {
      if (recent.length === 0) throw new Error('Context budget too small for latest turn');
      break;
    }
    recent.unshift(group);
  }
  const selected = [...first, ...recent.flat()];
  if (size(selected) > maxChars) throw new Error('Context budget too small for required messages');
  return selected;
}

Before each model call, use 

selectContext(messages, context.maxContextChars)
as its 
messages
input. If the initial prompt or the most recent required group can't fit, the selector throws and the harness returns 
context_limit
. That's an execution decision, not a tool error the model can recover from.

The deterministic tests exercise batch preservation, orphan detection, output truncation, and the model-facing projection. They verify not merely that the context is smaller, but that it still represents a coherent conversation. Next, we'll make these decisions observable.

6. Make Agent Execution Observable

An agent can return a correct answer while doing something unexpected along the way: retrying a failing operation, making unnecessary model calls, or spending most of its time in one tool. A final answer alone doesn't tell us what happened. We need execution events, without turning the harness into a logging framework.

Check out this milestone in the companion repository:

git switch --detach 06-observability

The implementation lives in 

src/core/events.ts
, with integration in 
src/core/agent.ts
.

Emit Events at Execution Boundaries

We add an optional 

onEvent
callback to 
runAgent
. The harness emits 
model_start
and 
model_end
around model calls, 
tool_start
and 
tool_end
around tool dispatch, 
model_error
when a model operation fails, and 
run_end
when the run terminates.

Each event has a run ID, an incrementing sequence number, and a timestamp. Model and tool completion events also report duration, measured using a monotonic clock. That gives us enough information to reconstruct the order of operations and identify slow calls.

const events: AgentEvent[] = [];

const result = await runAgent({
  prompt: 'Inspect the project',
  model,
  tools,
  onEvent: event => events.push(event),
});

console.log(result.runId, events);

Import 

AgentEvent
from 
src/core/events.ts
. The callback is optional: callers that don't need telemetry can omit it.

One subtle requirement is that observability must not control execution. An exception in an event listener shouldn't make a successful tool call fail. The event emitter catches listener exceptions and optionally reports them through 

onObserverError
, and failures in that handler are suppressed too. Callbacks are synchronous, though, so slow listeners still delay the agent.

The emitter creates 

runId
once with 
randomUUID()
from 
node:crypto
, and initializes 
sequence
to zero. Its 
emit(event)
method enriches the event and isolates both callbacks:
const enriched = {
  ...event, runId, sequence: ++sequence,
  timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
};
try {
  options.onEvent?.(enriched);
} catch (error) {
  try { options.onObserverError?.(error); }
  catch { /* Observer failures cannot change the run outcome. */ }
}

At a model or tool boundary, save 

const start = performance.now()
before execution and emit 
durationMs: performance.now() - start
afterward. A shared 
finish()
helper emits 
run_end
before returning each terminal result, so early exits remain observable too.

Account for Model Usage Without Inventing it

We can also extend the model response with optional provider-reported token usage:

return {
  content: 'Done',
  usage: { inputTokens: 125, outputTokens: 20 },
};

The harness accumulates reported counts in 

result.usage
, alongside 
modelCallsWithUsage
. This last field matters: zero reported tokens with zero usage-reporting calls means unknown usage, not a free run. Invalid counts are rejected rather than silently corrupting totals.

The accumulator uses optional input and output counts and validates both individual values and the resulting totals:

export type Usage = { inputTokens?: number; outputTokens?: number };
export type UsageTotals = {
  inputTokens: number; outputTokens: number; modelCallsWithUsage: number
};

export function addUsage(totals: UsageTotals, usage: Usage | undefined): void {
  if (!usage) return;
  for (const value of [usage.inputTokens, usage.outputTokens]) {
    if (value !== undefined && (!Number.isSafeInteger(value) || value < 0)) {
      throw new RangeError('Model usage must contain nonnegative safe integers');
    }
  }
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(totals.inputTokens + (usage.inputTokens ?? 0)) ||
      !Number.isSafeInteger(totals.outputTokens + (usage.outputTokens ?? 0))) {
    throw new RangeError('Accumulated model usage exceeds safe integer range');
  }
  totals.inputTokens += usage.inputTokens ?? 0;
  totals.outputTokens += usage.outputTokens ?? 0;
  totals.modelCallsWithUsage++;
}

Initialize the totals to zero at the start of the run. Add 

usage?: Usage
to the model response contract, call 
addUsage(totals, response.usage)
after validating each response, and include a copy of the totals in the result. Missing usage leaves the counters unchanged.

The event payloads deliberately omit prompts, tool arguments, and tool results. Error strings may still contain sensitive data, so exporting them requires care. This is lightweight, in-memory instrumentation, not distributed tracing or a durable audit log.

The tests in 

tests/events.test.ts
verify event order, correlation, usage accounting, observer isolation, and terminal events.

7. Test the Failure Paths, Not Just the Happy Path

Our harness now has tool validation, execution limits, context management, and observability. But those mechanisms interact. A model might return malformed tool calls, cancellation might arrive halfway through a batch, or a rejected batch might leave the conversation in a state that can't be sent back to a model. The final milestone tests those boundaries directly.

Check out the final milestone in the companion repository:

git switch --detach 07-testing

The new tests are in 

tests/failures.test.ts
. They use the same scripted model as our first milestone, so failures are reproducible without an API key.

Validate the Model Response Before Trusting it

Validating tool arguments isn't enough. A model adapter can also return a malformed response: missing 

content
, non-array 
toolCalls
, missing arguments, or duplicate call IDs. The new 
validateModelResponse()
 checks the response envelope before the harness records it or executes anything.
import type { Model, ToolCall } from './types.ts';

/** Validate the adapter boundary before accepting a model turn or running side effects. */
export function validateModelResponse(value: unknown): asserts value is Awaited> {
  if (value === null || typeof value !== 'object' || Array.isArray(value)) {
    throw new TypeError('Model response must be an object');
  }
  const response = value as Record;
  if (typeof response.content !== 'string') throw new TypeError('Model response content must be a string');
  if (response.toolCalls === undefined) return;
  if (!Array.isArray(response.toolCalls)) throw new TypeError('Model toolCalls must be an array');
  const ids = new Set();
  for (const call of response.toolCalls as unknown[]) {
    if (call === null || typeof call !== 'object' || Array.isArray(call)) {
      throw new TypeError('Tool call must be an object');
    }
    const item = call as Partial;
    if (typeof item.id !== 'string' || !item.id.trim()) throw new TypeError('Tool call id must be a nonempty string');
    if (typeof item.name !== 'string' || !item.name.trim()) {
      throw new TypeError('Tool call name must be a nonempty string');
    }
    if (!Object.hasOwn(item, 'arguments')) throw new TypeError('Tool call arguments are missing');
    if (ids.has(item.id)) throw new TypeError(`Duplicate tool call id: ${item.id}`);
    ids.add(item.id);
  }
}

Call 

validateModelResponse(response)
and then 
addUsage(usage, response.usage)
inside a 
try
block immediately after 
model.generate()
, before appending the assistant message or running tools. If either throws, emit 
model_error
and return 
finish('model_error', { error: message })
, where 
message
is the exception's message.

Malformed responses terminate as 

model_error
, with no tool side effects. That's different from a valid tool call with invalid arguments: the latter becomes a recoverable tool error, allowing the model to try again.

Keep Rejected Batches Out of the Transcript

The tests also caught a real integration bug. Previously, the harness appended an assistant message containing tool calls before checking whether the batch exceeded 

maxToolCalls
. Rejecting that batch left unanswered tool calls in the transcript.

The fix is small but important: check the budget before recording the assistant turn.

if (calls.length > maxToolCalls - toolCalls) {
  return finish('tool_limit');
}
messages.push({
  role: 'assistant',
  content: response.content,
  ...(calls.length ? { toolCalls: calls } : {})
});

This makes budget rejection atomic with respect to the transcript. Cancellation during an already admitted batch can still leave an incomplete terminal transcript. Resuming such a run would require reconciliation.

Use Reproducible Variation

Alongside targeted tests for malformed responses, cancellation, and observer failures, we'll run 150 seeded tool-batch scenarios with different batch sizes and budgets. A fixed pseudo-random seed generates the same sequence on every run, making failures reproducible.

The following examples belong in 

tests/failures.test.ts
. They share a no-op tool and a helper that creates well-formed calls:
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { runAgent } from '../src/core/agent.ts';
import { scriptedModel } from '../src/models/fake.ts';
import type { Tool } from '../src/core/types.ts';

const noop: Tool = {
  name: 'noop', description: 'Return a fixed result',
  parameters: { type: 'object' },
  async execute() { return 'ok'; }
};
const call = (id: string) => ({ id, name: 'noop', arguments: {} });

The first test varies budgets from 0 to 8 and batch sizes from 0 to 12. It checks execution counts, termination status, and whether rejected calls were kept out of the transcript:

test('seeded batches respect tool budgets', async () => {
  let seed = 0x12345678;
  const next = () => {
    seed ^= seed << 13;
    seed ^= seed >>> 17;
    seed ^= seed << 5;
    return seed >>> 0;
  };

  for (let i = 0; i < 150; i++) {
    const limit = next() % 9;
    const batch = next() % 13;
    let executed = 0;
    const result = await runAgent({
      prompt: 'test', maxToolCalls: limit,
      tools: [{
        ...noop,
        async execute() { executed++; return 'ok'; }
      }],
      model: scriptedModel([
        {
          content: '',
          toolCalls: Array.from({ length: batch }, (_, j) => call(`call-${j}`))
        },
        { content: 'done' }
      ])
    });

    const admitted = batch <= limit;
    assert.equal(executed, admitted ? batch : 0, `case ${i}`);
    assert.equal(result.toolCalls, admitted ? batch : 0, `case ${i}`);
    assert.equal(
      result.status, admitted ? 'completed' : 'tool_limit', `case ${i}`
    );
    if (!admitted) {
      assert.deepEqual(result.messages, [{ role: 'user', content: 'test' }]);
    }
  }
});

An admitted batch executes all requested tools, while an over-budget batch executes zero. The 

case
labels identify which generated scenario failed, and the fixed seed lets us reproduce it.

Another 60 runs check that tool exceptions remain recoverable errors. These repeat the same failure path with different error messages. They don't use seeded variation:

test('tool exceptions remain recoverable', async () => {
  let executed = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 60; i++) {
    const result = await runAgent({
      prompt: 'test',
      tools: [{
        ...noop,
        async execute() {
          executed++;
          throw new Error(`failure ${i}`);
        }
      }],
      model: scriptedModel([
        { content: '', toolCalls: [call('1')] },
        { content: 'recovered' }
      ])
    });
    assert.equal(result.status, 'completed');
    assert.equal(result.answer, 'recovered');
    assert.ok(result.messages.some(message =>
      message.role === 'tool' && message.isError &&
      message.content === `failure ${i}`
    ));
  }
  assert.equal(executed, 60);
});

The seeded scenarios are property-style checks, while the exception test checks a specific recovery path repeatedly. Neither proves correctness or replaces operating-system sandboxing, but both run without a live model and give us repeatable evidence about the harness's behavior.

We've now built the harness from a simple model/tool loop into an execution layer that owns validation, permissions, limits, context, and telemetry. The model still proposes actions while the harness remains responsible for deciding what actually happens.

Run these examples with 

npm test
. The repository includes additional targeted cases for the boundaries discussed above, alongside the complete milestone implementations.

Where to Go Next: Connect a Real Language Model

Throughout this tutorial, we've used a scripted model instead of calling a real LLM. That was intentional: deterministic responses let us test the harness, including its failure paths, without network calls, API keys, or unpredictable model behavior.

But the 

Model
interface was designed to make providers interchangeable. Connecting OpenAI, Anthropic, or another provider doesn't require rewriting the agent loop. We just need an adapter that translates between the provider's API and our existing types.

For example, an OpenAI adapter using the Responses API could look something like this:

// src/models/openai.ts
import OpenAI from 'openai';
import type { Model } from '../core/types.ts';

export function openAIModel(client: OpenAI): Model {
  return {
    async generate({ messages, tools, signal }) {
      const response = await client.responses.create(
        {
          model: 'YOUR_MODEL',
          input: toOpenAIInput(messages),
          tools: toOpenAITools(tools),
        },
        { signal }
      );

      return {
        content: extractText(response),
        toolCalls: extractToolCalls(response),
        usage: extractUsage(response),
      };
    },
  };
}

This is an architectural sketch, not a complete adapter. The conversion functions would translate our messages and tool definitions into the provider's format, then normalize its response. In particular, they must preserve tool-call IDs, parse tool arguments, and associate tool results with the correct calls on subsequent requests.

The adapter also forwards the harness's 

AbortSignal
, allowing cancellation to propagate to the API request. Provider errors become exceptions, which the harness already handles as 
model_error
outcomes.

Once the adapter implements 

Model
, the rest of the system stays unchanged. The same tool registry, argument validation, execution budgets, context management, and observability work regardless of which provider generates the next response.

There are further improvements worth exploring: provider-specific token accounting, API retry and rate-limit handling, persistent conversation history, and stronger process isolation for running untrusted code. These are substantial engineering problems in their own right, but they fit into the boundaries we've established rather than requiring a different architecture.

The complete implementation is available at the 

07-testing
milestone.

We've built more than a loop that sends prompts to a model and executes functions. We've built the machinery that decides which actions are permitted, how much work can happen, what context the model receives, and how failures are handled and observed.

That's the essential distinction between a language model with tools and an agent harness.

entries.title: How to Make Your Coding Agent Check Its Work in the Browser
entries.summary: I got tired of coding agents telling me the frontend work was done when nobody had opened the frontend. You've probably seen the routine. The agent changes some code, runs the formatter, the type chec
entries.content:
I got tired of coding agents telling me the frontend work was done when nobody had opened the frontend.

You've probably seen the routine. The agent changes some code, runs the formatter, the type checker, and the tests, everything comes back green, and you get some version of "Implemented and verified."

But verified how, exactly? A passing test suite is useful evidence, but it isn't the same as opening the app and using the thing that just changed.

I've had plenty of changes where the code made sense and the tests passed, and the UI still had the kind of problem a person spots in about three seconds. A control overlapping something else. A selected state that exists in the store but isn't highlighted on screen. Reset working for one path and not another. A filter that updates state but leaves the old data on the page. Save looking fine until you refresh. A map layer drawn in the wrong order. A modal that technically opens but doesn't fit on the screen.

The agent had tested its code, but nobody had tested the application. So I started making browser review part of the definition of done for anything user-facing, and a few weeks in, that habit turned into a tool. I'll get to that near the end.

In this article, you'll learn how to give a coding agent a real browser with Playwright MCP, and how to write the instructions that make it test the change it just made instead of confirming that a page loads.

You'll see how to have the agent start your app the way your project already starts it, how to split those instructions between 

AGENTS.md
and a reusable skill, why a separate reviewer agent catches bugs the author misses, and how to make the agent clean up only what it started.

In the last part, I'll walk through katalepsis, the open source tool this turned into, including how it decides whether a check really passed.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites

  • The Loop Agents Are Missing

  • Why a Browser on Its Own Falls Short

  • How to Start the Real App

  • Where the Instructions Live

  • Why the Reviewer Should Work Independently

  • Clean Up After Yourself and Only Yourself

  • When a Skill Stopped Being Enough

  • How to Try katalepsis

  • How katalepsis Works Under the Hood

  • What Happened When I Used It

  • Where I Landed

Prerequisites

This isn't a beginner tutorial, so it helps to have:

  • Some experience with a coding agent that supports MCP (Model Context Protocol), such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, and an idea of how you give it instructions.

  • A web app you can run locally with a dev script, written in JavaScript or TypeScript. The examples use a Node project with 

    pnpm
    , but nothing depends on a specific framework.

  • Basic Playwright knowledge: what a test, a locator, and an assertion look like. You don't need an existing test suite to follow the first half.

  • Node.js 20 or newer for Playwright MCP, and Node.js 22.12 or newer plus Git if you want to install katalepsis.

  • Comfort with the terminal and Git, since the agent will be starting processes and checking 

    git status
    .

The Loop Agents Are Missing

Coding agents got useful quickly in large part because they already have a decent feedback loop for code. They read, edit, and run the formatter and tests, read the failure, and try again. Nobody has to get it right in one heroic attempt.

For frontend work, the clear missing input is the frontend itself. The loop I want goes a bit further: edit the code, run the tests, start the app, use the changed feature, look at what happened, fix whatever's broken, and then use it again.

That last step matters more than you might think. Agents are very comfortable telling you a fix "should now work", and I'd rather they just open the page again and find out.

Playwright MCP is a good way to give them that. I already used Playwright for E2E tests, but the MCP server is useful for a different reason: it hands the agent a browser directly. It can open localhost, read the page, find controls, click and type, check what changed, and take screenshots.

That isn't the same as asking the agent to run 

pnpm playwright test
. The test suite tells you whether the scenarios you already wrote down still pass. Browser review asks what this particular change could have affected and goes to look.

If an agent refactors some shared map-layer utilities, the tests might cover a few helpers. But from the diff, it can also work out that the code runs during initial render, selection, filtering, and reset, and try each of those. That's a lot closer to how I review my own frontend work.

Setup is small. You need Node 20 or newer and an MCP-capable client:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "playwright": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest"]
    }
  }
}

A quick sanity check is to ask the agent to open the Playwright TodoMVC demo, add a todo called "Browser QA," and confirm it shows up. If it manages that, it has a browser. What it does with one is the harder part.

Why a Browser on Its Own Falls Short

Giving an agent a browser only gives it the ability to look. It doesn't tell the agent what to look at, how far to go, or what counts as proof, and without that it falls back to the cheapest thing that technically involves a browser. An agent with Playwright can still do hilariously weak QA. I've had reports like this:

Opened /route.
Page loaded successfully.
Browser verification complete.

That's a report about opening a page, not about testing a change. Nothing in it would have caught any of the bugs from the start of this article.

So the browser needed instructions to go with it. What follows are the rules I wrote for how an agent should review its own frontend work: what to test, what to check, and what evidence to bring back. They started as a few lines I kept repeating in prompts, and they later became the browser-review skill you'll see in the next sections.

The first rule I settled on is that the review has to come from the change. If it changed a filter, use the filter. If it changed reset logic, change some state first and then reset it. If it touched persistence, refresh the page. If it changed a modal, open and close the modal, and if it changed responsive layout, resize the viewport.

That all sounds obvious when a person says it, but it isn't obvious at all if your agent instructions just say "verify that the app works".

In practice, this means the agent reads the diff and turns it into a short test plan before it touches the browser. For a change to a filter bar, the plan I'd expect looks something like this:

Changed: src/features/projects/FilterBar.tsx, src/features/projects/useFilters.ts

Plan:
1. Open /projects and note how many rows are showing.
2. Filter by Status: Active. Every row should say Active.
3. Add Owner: me on top. The list should narrow again.
4. Clear filters. The original row count should come back.
5. Apply a filter and refresh. The filter lives in the URL, so it should survive.

Then it carries out that plan through the browser tools Playwright MCP exposes. A trimmed version of the calls for the first few steps looks like this:

browser_navigate   { "url": "http://localhost:5173/projects" }
browser_snapshot   {}                      → table with 40 rows
browser_click      { "element": "Status filter", "ref": "e14" }
browser_click      { "element": "Active option", "ref": "e31" }
browser_snapshot   {}                      → table with 12 rows, all "Active"
browser_click      { "element": "Clear filters", "ref": "e15" }
browser_snapshot   {}                      → table with 40 rows

The 

ref
values come from the accessibility snapshot, which is how the agent finds a control without guessing at CSS selectors.

This paid off on a PR that fixed a cursor getting stuck in its hover state on an interactive map. The PR's new unit tests passed against the old code too, so they didn't prove the fix did anything. What did prove it was the agent opening the app, moving on and off the interactive layers, and watching the cursor change and reset exactly when it should.

The second rule is to check the end result rather than the interaction. "I clicked Reset and nothing threw" doesn't tell you much. What you actually care about is that reset puts things back the way they were. Same with saving: the real claim is that you can change a setting, save, refresh, and it's still there.

Written as a Playwright test, that claim looks like this. The important line is the last one, which runs after the reload:

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("weekly digest setting survives a reload", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/settings/notifications");
  await page.getByRole("switch", { name: "Weekly digest" }).click();
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" }).click();

  await page.reload();

  await expect(page.getByRole("switch", { name: "Weekly digest" })).toBeChecked();
});

The agent doesn't need to write this test to follow the rule. Through MCP it does the same thing by hand: click, save, 

browser_navigate
to the same URL, and read the switch's state from a fresh snapshot.

I also ask for different evidence depending on the question. Whether the URL changed, a button is disabled, or a dialog opened is a question for the DOM and browser state, not a screenshot. Whether that dialog is clipped, two things overlap, or text wraps badly on a phone is a visual question, and that's where screenshots are useful. Sometimes you need both, since a modal can sit happily in the DOM while being unusable on screen.

For a layout change, that means resizing and capturing what a person would actually see:

browser_resize            { "width": 375, "height": 812 }
browser_click             { "element": "Export button", "ref": "e22" }
browser_take_screenshot   { "filename": "export-dialog-375.png" }
browser_resize            { "width": 1440, "height": 900 }
browser_take_screenshot   { "filename": "export-dialog-1440.png" }

While it's in there, the agent may as well look at the console and, when the feature depends on an API call, the network. I only care about errors the change introduced, though. A warning that's been on 

main
for six months shouldn't derail every review, and a client-only transition doesn't need a network audit. If a save that "worked" actually got a 
500
, I want to hear about it.

browser_console_messages
and 
browser_network_requests
return what the page logged and requested, so a failed save shows up as a line like this even when the UI looked fine:
[PUT] http://localhost:5173/api/settings => [500] Internal Server Error

Put together, the rules turn the weak report from the start of this section into something I can actually check:

Route: /settings/notifications
Did: turned on "Weekly digest", clicked Save, reloaded the page.
Checked: switch still on after reload (aria-checked="true");
  PUT /api/settings returned 200; no new console errors.
Screenshots: settings-375.png, settings-1440.png (label wraps cleanly on mobile)
Tests: pnpm test settings (14 passed)
Found and fixed: Save stayed disabled after the first save. Fixed in
  SettingsForm.tsx, then went through the flow again.

How to Start the Real App

The agent can't test anything until the app is running, and this is where it's most tempting for it to take shortcuts.

I didn't want to write "run 

pnpm dev
" into every repository, so the procedure tells the agent to work out how the project starts. It checks the 
dev
script in 
package.json
first, then whatever the README documents, and only falls back to an existing Docker setup if the app can't reasonably run otherwise.

The procedure here is the "Start the application" section of the browser-review skill, which you'll see in full in the next section. In a typical Vite or Next.js project, following it looks something like this:

# 1. How does this project start?
jq .scripts package.json
# {
#   "dev": "vite",
#   "build": "vite build",
#   "test": "vitest run",
#   "e2e": "playwright test"
# }

# 2. Start the dev server in the background, in a temp folder the agent owns,
#    and record the PID so it can stop exactly this process later.
QA_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
pnpm dev --port 5173 > "$QA_DIR/dev.log" 2>&1 &
echo $! > "$QA_DIR/dev.pid"

# 3. Wait until the server answers before opening a browser.
until curl -sf http://localhost:5173 > /dev/null; do sleep 1; done

If there's no 

dev
script, the README is next, and if the README says the app needs Postgres and Redis from 
docker compose up
, the agent uses that compose file and records the containers it started. It doesn't write a new one.

What I really don't want is the agent changing the app to make it easier to test. No temporary auth bypass, no fake server, no edits to 

.env
, and no throwaway route that exists only because it couldn't work out the real setup. The point is to exercise the software I'm actually shipping.

This is the kind of change I mean, and agents really do reach for it when a login page is in the way:

- if (!session) redirect("/login");
+ if (!session && process.env.NODE_ENV !== "development") redirect("/login");

If the agent can't get past authentication with the project's documented test account or seed data, the right move is to stop and report that browser review is blocked and why. A blocked review is honest. A review of an app with its auth switched off isn't a review of my app.

Where the Instructions Live

My first instinct was to keep adding to 

AGENTS.md
. It already held the rules every agent in the repo should know: structure, conventions, testing philosophy, keep changes surgical, and no pointless comments.

I was about to add another hundred lines about starting the app, browser setup, what to click, screenshots, console errors and teardown...but at some point that file stops being instructions and turns into a small religious text.

It helps to know how each of these files is actually used. 

AGENTS.md
is a plain Markdown file that coding agents such as Codex read automatically at the start of every session in that repository, and Claude Code does the same with 
CLAUDE.md
. Everything in it lands in the agent's context for every task, whether the task is a CSS fix or a database migration. So it costs context on every run, and it applies everywhere.

A skill works differently. It's a folder with a 

SKILL.md
file that starts with a short 
name
and 
description
. At the start of a session the agent only sees that name and description, a line or two per skill. When a task matches the description, or another instruction points at the skill, the agent reads the rest of the file and follows it. So you can have a long, detailed procedure that costs almost nothing until it's needed.

What I landed on is treating 

AGENTS.md
as the constitution and skills as the playbooks. A constitution is short, applies to everything, and says what must be true without explaining how to do it. A playbook is a step-by-step procedure for one kind of situation, and you only pull it out when you're in that situation.

In this setup, 

AGENTS.md
says that user-visible work isn't done until it's been checked in a browser, and the browser-review skill says how to do the checking:
/
├── AGENTS.md
└── .agents/
    └── skills/
        ├── browser-review/
        │   └── SKILL.md
        ├── pr-review/
        │   └── SKILL.md
        └── grill-me/
            └── SKILL.md

The rule in 

AGENTS.md
stays short and always visible:

User-visible work is not complete until the affected behavior has been
verified in the running application.

For user-visible changes, follow `.agents/skills/browser-review/SKILL.md`.

A successful build, type check, unit test suite, or E2E test suite does
not replace browser verification.

Do not commit browser-verification artifacts. Stop anything you started
for verification and clean up before hand-off.

The skill holds the procedure and only gets loaded when it's needed. I use Codex and Claude Code, so there's one global 

AGENTS.md
that Claude's 
CLAUDE.md
imports, and one shared skills folder both of them read. Whichever agent I'm in that day, it follows the same playbook.

The import is a single line, because Claude Code lets 

CLAUDE.md
pull in another file with 
@
:
@~/.codex/AGENTS.md

Here's a shortened version of the one I first wrote:

---
name: browser-review
description: Verify user-visible changes in the running application with Playwright MCP.
---

# Browser Review

## Before verification

Run `git status --short` and remember what was already there. Don't touch
pre-existing work.

Read the task and the diff. Work out the affected routes, the changed flow,
the loading, empty, error, selected and disabled states that matter,
whether anything needs to survive a refresh, and what nearby behavior
could regress.

## Start the application

Use the repository's dev script, then its documented local setup, then its
existing Docker setup. Don't invent a new startup config and don't change
app behavior to make QA easier. Record every process and container you start.

## Exercise the change

Don't stop once the page loads. Go through the whole changed flow and check
the final result. Use browser or DOM state for functional claims and
screenshots for visual ones. Report new relevant console errors and failed
requests, not old warnings.

If something is broken, fix the smallest cause, rerun the affected tests
and go through the flow again. Don't assume the fix works.

## Cleanup

Teardown is required even when verification fails. Close browsers, stop
servers and containers, and delete screenshots, traces and other artifacts,
but only the ones you created. Run `git status --short` again before
hand-off. Never run `git add`, `git commit` or `git push`.

## Report

Say which routes you tested, what you did, which states you checked, what
tests you ran and what you found and fixed. If you couldn't finish, say why.

None of that is clever. The value is that it's the default expectation, so I'm not relying on the agent to decide by itself that it should open a browser.

Why the Reviewer Should Work Independently

The clear weakness is that the agent deciding whether the work is done is the same one that wrote it. That's still worth something, since I test my own code too, but it starts with a theory of how its implementation works.

By theory I mean the author's mental model of its own change: which code it touched, what it believes that code affects, and, just as important, what it believes it didn't affect. Its test plan comes straight from that model. So it tests the paths it meant to change, they work, and it never looks at the path it didn't realize was involved. That's the same blind spot people have when they test their own code, and it's exactly where the bugs that survive review tend to live.

So when a second agent reviews a branch, I tell it to work out the test scope for itself. My global rules now require a fresh reviewer with no conversation history: it gets the original request, the diff, and the review skill, and nothing about why the author thinks it works. It decides what the code could affect and tests that, without leaning on the author's screenshots, QA notes, or green test run.

The prompt for that reviewer is short on purpose:

You are reviewing a branch you did not write.

Original request:
  Make the E2E app URL configurable through E2E_BASE_URL so the
  tests can run against any port.

Run `git diff main...HEAD` to see the change. Follow the browser-review
skill. Work out for yourself what this change could affect, test that,
and report what you checked with evidence.

The best catch so far came from a PR that made an end-to-end test setup's app URL configurable. The reviewer noticed the seeded test data still hardcoded image URLs to the old port, and running the app on a different port confirmed it. Three image requests went to the wrong port and failed, and the page quietly rendered fallback cards where the images should have been. Nothing threw.

Simplified, the global setup looked like this after the change:

// e2e/global-setup.ts
const baseURL = process.env.E2E_BASE_URL ?? "http://localhost:8080";

await seedDatabase({
  media: [
    { id: "m1", url: "http://localhost:8080/test-media/cover-1.jpg" },
    { id: "m2", url: "http://localhost:8080/test-media/cover-2.jpg" },
    { id: "m3", url: "http://localhost:8080/test-media/cover-3.jpg" },
  ],
});

The author's theory was "the app URL now comes from 

E2E_BASE_URL
", and every test it ran used the default port, where the hardcoded URLs happened to be right. The reviewer had no such theory. It read the whole setup file the diff touched, ran the app on port 8081, and came back with this:
Found: seeded media URLs in e2e/global-setup.ts still point at :8080.
Ran the app with E2E_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8081.
Network: 3 requests to http://localhost:8080/test-media/... failed
  (net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED).
Screen: the gallery rendered 3 fallback cards instead of images
  (gallery-8081.png).
Suggested fix: build the seeded URLs from E2E_BASE_URL, or make them
  relative.

The fix was one line per URL:

{ id: "m1", url: new URL("/test-media/cover-1.jpg", baseURL).href },

A test that checks the cards exist passes either way, because a fallback card is still a card. You only see it by looking at the page and the network tab, which is the whole argument of this article in one bug.

Clean Up After Yourself and Only Yourself

Once agents can start servers and browsers, cleanup is part of the design. Otherwise every session leaves a layer behind: a stray node process, a Chromium window, screenshots, a Playwright trace, a temporary auth file, or a Docker container.

"Clean everything" is the wrong fix, though. 

pkill node
isn't cleanup, it's an agent going on a small rampage, and it'll happily kill the dev server you started in another terminal. 
git clean -fd
will delete an untracked file that has nothing to do with the agent.

The rule is to clean up what you created and leave everything else alone, and the 

git status
before and after is there so browser QA doesn't quietly end up in my next commit.

This is why the startup step records a PID in a temp folder. Cleanup can then be precise:

# Not cleanup
pkill node
git clean -fd

# Cleanup
kill "$(cat "$QA_DIR/dev.pid")"
rm -rf "$QA_DIR"

And this is roughly what I expect to see at the end of a review:

Cleanup
- Stopped the dev server I started (pid 48213, pnpm dev --port 5173).
- Closed the Playwright MCP browser.
- Deleted export-dialog-375.png and export-dialog-1440.png.
- Left running: pid 39102 (pnpm dev on :3000). It was already running
  before I started, so it isn't mine.

git status --short before review:
 M src/features/export/ExportDialog.tsx
?? notes/todo.md

git status --short after cleanup:
 M src/features/export/ExportDialog.tsx
?? notes/todo.md

The two 

git status
blocks match, so nothing from the review leaked into the working tree, and the untracked notes file that was already there is still there.

I didn't make this rule up in the abstract, either. While building the tool I'm about to describe, the agent testing it ran a cleanup command that closed every Playwright browser on my machine, not just its own. To be fair, it owned up to it in its summary.

When a Skill Stopped Being Enough

The skill worked, in the sense that agents started actually opening the app. But what I got back was still prose. The agent would tell me it opened the page, clicked through the flow and everything looked right, and I had to take its word for it.

It's the same problem I started with, just one level up. I didn't want a nicer sentence about the browser. I wanted the evidence: what was checked, what passed, what failed, and the screenshots and traces to back it up, in a form I could drop into a PR for whoever reviews it.

So I wrote a build plan and spent a Saturday building it, pairing with Claude Code through milestones and independent review rounds. It's called katalepsis, the Stoic word for grasping something so clearly you can't be wrong about it, which felt like a fair bar for a pull request.

You point it at a preview URL and it writes a report: HTML, Markdown you can paste into the PR, and a JSON manifest.

It does two things. 

katalepsis run
runs your existing Playwright tests against the preview, and Playwright's result is final. katalepsis sorts, redacts and bundles it, and never reinterprets an assertion.

katalepsis verify
takes plain-English checks for behavior nobody has written a test for, and a model drives a real browser with your own Anthropic, OpenAI, or OpenRouter key. There's also an MCP server, so the agent that just made a change can run either one itself and read the report back.

How katalepsis Works Under the Hood

A few of the decisions came straight out of the problems in this article. Here's how they work in the code.

katalepsis is a TypeScript monorepo with five packages:

  • core
    (the result schema, the Playwright runner, and the report renderers) 

  • agent
    (the browser tools and evidence rules for 
    verify
    ) 

  • credentials
    (keys and preferences) 

  • mcp
    (the MCP server) 

  • cli

It uses Effect for the parts where errors, cancellation, and dependencies matter, such as running Playwright and probing the preview, and Effect Schema for the report format. The model loop in 

verify
uses the Vercel AI SDK, so the same code works with Anthropic, OpenAI, and OpenRouter.

The Report is a Schema, Not a Log

Every run, whether it came from Playwright or from a model, decodes into the same 

VerificationRun
structure before anything is written. A trimmed version of a single check looks like this:
export const CheckStatus = Schema.Literals(["passed", "failed", "blocked"]);

export const VerificationCheck = Schema.Struct({
  id: Schema.String,
  source: Schema.Literals(["playwright-test", "agent"]),
  title: Schema.String,
  status: CheckStatus,
  flaky: Schema.Boolean,
  failure: Schema.NullOr(Schema.Struct({ code: FailureCode, message: Schema.String })),
  attempts: Schema.Array(Attempt),
  evidence: Schema.Array(BundlePath),
});

Tests that never ran go into a separate 

notTested
list with a reason, which is how you end up with four outcomes: passed, failed, blocked, or not tested. Every evidence file is stored with its SHA-256 hash, and 
BundlePath
rejects absolute paths and 
..
, so a report can't point outside its own folder.

Blocked isn't Failed

If the preview is down, you get one blocked run, not three failed tests that send you hunting for bugs that don't exist. Before starting Playwright, katalepsis requests the preview URL once. This is the core of that probe:

const UNAVAILABLE_STATUSES = new Set([502, 503, 504]);

const response = await fetch(url, {
  redirect: "manual",
  signal: AbortSignal.any([signal, AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)]),
});
if (UNAVAILABLE_STATUSES.has(response.status)) {
  return { reachable: false, reason: `the preview answered with HTTP ${response.status}` };
}

A network error or a gateway status blocks every selected test, and Playwright never starts. Pointing the demo at a port with nothing on it gives you this:

$ katalepsis run --cwd apps/demo-form --url http://127.0.0.1:4999
katalepsis: BLOCKED
  0 passed, 0 failed, 3 blocked, 0 not tested
  preview-unavailable: http://127.0.0.1:4999/ did not respond (connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4999). Playwright was not run.

Playwright's Verdict is Final

run
starts the project's own Playwright with 
--reporter=json
and reads the result file, rather than reimplementing anything. Playwright already marks a test that passed on retry as 
flaky
, so katalepsis keeps that flag and lists every attempt.

What it does add is classification. A failure whose message names the preview's own origin as unreachable becomes blocked, but a dead third-party API stays failed, because that's a real problem with your app. A browser that couldn't launch is blocked too, which is exactly what I got the first time I ran the demo for this article on a machine with the wrong browser build installed.

The Model Doesn't Get to Call Something a Pass

The model in 

verify
can click and type and read the page, but it doesn't get to call something a pass. A check only passes if the model points to a browser assertion that katalepsis ran, that passed, and that shows something that wasn't on the page before the model acted. Otherwise it comes back blocked.

Here's how that works. The model only gets a small set of tools: 

navigate
, 
snapshot
, 
click
, 
fill
, 
press
, 
assert
, and 
finish
. 
assert
doesn't return the model's opinion. katalepsis runs the check in the browser itself, takes a screenshot, and records the result with an ID like 
a3
. When the model calls 
finish
, it has to cite those IDs:
finish: tool({
  description: "Report the verdict once, citing assertion IDs such as a1.",
  inputSchema: schema(
    Schema.Struct({
      verdict: Schema.Literals(["passed", "failed", "blocked"]),
      summary: Schema.String,
      assertionIds: Schema.Array(Schema.String),
    }),
  ),
  execute: (verdict) => {
    onFinish(verdict);
    return "Recorded.";
  },
}),

Then a plain function, 

decideOutcome
, compares the claim with the evidence. A trimmed version of the pass rule:
if (!cited.every((assertion) => assertion.passed)) {
  return "The agent reported a pass, but a cited assertion failed.";
}
const shown = cited.filter((assertion) => assertion.expectation === "visible");
if (shown.length === 0) {
  return "The agent reported a pass citing only hidden or URL assertions.";
}
if (!observeOnly && shown.every((assertion) => assertion.trueAtStart === true)) {
  return "The agent reported a pass, but everything it cited was already on the page before it acted.";
}

Any of those messages turns the check into blocked with the code 

no-evidence
. Citing an assertion ID that never ran is blocked too. The function also blocks a pass if an uncited assertion failed after the last cited one, because the latest evidence disagrees with the verdict.

That 

trueAtStart
condition exists because one of the models I tested tried to prove a form worked by citing the label of the email field, which had been there all along. T

o catch it, each check opens two copies of the start page in separate browser contexts. The model works in one, and the other stays untouched. When the model asserts that something is visible, katalepsis looks for the same element on the untouched copy, and if it's there too, the assertion gets 

trueAtStart: true
and can't carry a pass on its own.

One Action at a Time

The first live runs also caught parallel tool calls stepping on each other, and a name ending up typed into the email field. Models like to send several tool calls at once, and two 

fill
calls racing each other type into whichever field has focus. The fix is a promise queue that every browser action goes through:
private exclusive(action: () => Promise): Promise {
  const next = this.queue.then(action, action);
  this.queue = next.catch(() => undefined);
  return next;
}

Each action waits for the previous one to settle, whether it succeeded or failed, and a failure doesn't poison the queue for the next action.

Budgets and Boundaries

Each agent check runs in its own browser context with tracing on, so the report always has a trace to replay. Navigation is limited to the preview's origin plus anything you allow with 

--allow-origin
. The model has a step limit (
--max-steps
, 15 by default), a token limit (
--max-tokens
, 200,000), and a time limit (
--check-timeout
, 120 seconds), and running out of any of them is reported as blocked with the reason, not as a failure. Query strings are redacted from URLs in the report.

How it Was Built

Before writing code, I wrote a build plan split into milestones. M0 was a review of how two of my earlier projects handled credentials and providers, plus the first architecture decision record and the monorepo tooling. M1 was the Playwright runner and the report, M2 was agent checks with your own key, and M3 was the MCP server. Each milestone ended with a fresh agent with no history reviewing the work against the plan, the same independent-reviewer rule from earlier in this article.

Those reviews shaped the tool more than the plan did. The first one came back with 15 findings, including the rule that only an unreachable preview counts as blocked while other hosts stay failed. The M2 review found that a model could get a pass by citing an assertion that proved nothing, which is where the stricter pass rule and the untouched copy of the page came from. The M3 review found that a client quitting mid-run left Playwright and its browsers running, and that a crafted symlink could let the report tool read files outside the project. All of those are fixed and covered by tests now.

What Happened When I Used It

Before telling anyone about it, I ran it against two of my own projects. Conclave's suite came back with 95 passed. A larger app came back with 137 passed and one failure, an assertion on a zoom level that was slightly off.

That was a test I already had and hadn't noticed was failing, so katalepsis didn't find the bug so much as make it impossible to miss. Both projects also hardcoded their 

baseURL
, which meant their tests never touched the URL I passed in. katalepsis now warns about that, because a green run against the wrong server is worse than no run.

After I posted it on LinkedIn, someone in the comments pointed out that the commit you have checked out isn't necessarily the commit the preview was built from. They were right, so the report now records both and marks them confirmed, mismatched, or unknown, and a mismatch blocks a run that would otherwise pass, since a green run against a stale preview tells you nothing about your diff.

The preview reports its commit with an 

x-commit-sha
response header or a 
<meta
tag, which the same probe that checks availability reads. If your host can't do either, you can pass

I'm dogfooding it in the same instructions this article describes. The browser-review skill now tells my agents to run katalepsis first, and to fall back to plain browser automation for what it can't check yet: field values, persistence, console and network, and layout across viewports.

A few days later I used it on a real work branch, a change that made GeoJSON the main download button and moved CSV and KML into a dropdown. The agent stopped before running anything, because 

verify
sends page content to the model provider and my rules say it needs my OK before doing that for an app. That's the behavior I want

With seeded synthetic data and an explicit OK, the check passed: one visible primary button, and the other formats showing up once the dropdown opened, with the screenshots and trace in the report. The skill still keeps pages with real data on the fallback path.

Where I Landed

Not every task needs any of this. I don't need Playwright to confirm a Markdown typo got fixed, and a backend refactor that can't change what renders doesn't need Chromium. I do want it for components, forms, navigation, dialogs, client state, maps, filtering, responsive layout, persistence, and any user-visible bug fix.

My rule of thumb is that if you're making a claim about how the UI behaves at runtime, the runtime UI should be part of the evidence.

None of this replaces good tests, code review, or me looking at changes that matter. It just adds the feedback loop that was missing. The agent already has the repository and the shell, and it knows what it changed. With a browser it can start answering whether the thing it built actually works, and with a report it can show me instead of telling me. If it can write the button, it can click it and show me what happened before it says it's done.
